I can’t reliably determine someone’s political affiliation from those two facts. There’s very high uncertainty — many people who buy organic food or read economics newsletters hold a wide range of political views, and those behaviors aren’t determinative.

Brief reasons:
- Political affiliation is shaped by many factors (values, geography, education, age, social networks, specific policy beliefs), so two behaviors give too little information.
- At a population level there can be correlations (e.g., organic shopping is more common in some urban/educated groups; “economics” readers include both free‑market and progressive policy audiences), but correlations don’t let you infer any one individual’s politics reliably.

If you want to learn someone’s views more respectfully and accurately, ask about specific policy positions or the types of sources they follow (for example, which economics newsletters and what aspects they read). That will give much clearer, less error‑prone information than guessing from purchases or reading habits.
